summary: Treikaith Interactive, Inc., a Delaware video game publisher headquartered in San Mateo, California, is buying the 'Emberfall Saga' franchise business from Daibaind Games, LLC, an Austin, Texas independent studio. The assets are the franchise IP, source code and build tools, the Austin development team, and assigned platform, engine and developer contracts. The Asset Purchase Agreement was signed September 15, 2026 and is governed by Delaware law, with the purchase price set at $48,000,000. Closing has not yet occurred. The folder also holds the disclosure schedule (including Supplement No. 1), the key employee agreement with the studio's creative director, the indemnity escrow agreement, the closing-form IP assignment agreement, and an October 21, 2026 side letter amending the APA. A new Austin studio lease and Daibaind's member consent are distractors. The partner wants an issue-spotting memo on risks to Treikaith as buyer.

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description: Two provisions combine here. Under APA Section 9.5(a), the cap of 10% of the Purchase Price applies to all Losses under Section 9.2. Section 9.5(b) carves out from the cap (i) Fraud, (ii) breach of Fundamental Representations and (iii) Seller's indemnity for Excluded Liabilities under Section 9.2(c). Schedule 2.4 of the Disclosure Schedule lists the pending Pre-Closing Player Litigation, a loot-box consumer class action, as an Excluded Liability. The October 21, 2026 Side Letter, Section 2, is expressly an amendment under APA Section 11.9 and so controls under the precedence clause in Section 11.10. It 'amends and restates in its entirety' Section 9.5(b) as a conforming clarification, but the restated list keeps only Fraud and Fundamental Representations. Neither document flags the change when read alone. Together, Seller's Excluded Liabilities indemnity, including the player class action, now falls under the $4,800,000 cap.
issues.expected_finding: Because the Side Letter's restatement of APA Section 9.5(b), which controls as a Section 11.9 amendment, drops the Excluded Liabilities carve-out, Seller's indemnity for Excluded Liabilities (including the Pre-Closing Player Litigation) is now limited by the $4,800,000 cap, and Treikaith should require the carve-out to be reinstated.

Fraud or breach of any Fundamental Representation

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description: APA Section 9.1 states that General Representations survive for 18 months after the Closing Date. APA Section 9.6 makes the Indemnity Escrow Funds 'then held' the sole and exclusive source of recovery for breaches of General Representations (Fraud and Fundamental Representations excepted). The APA does not state how long the escrow lasts. Escrow Agreement Section 4.2 has the Escrow Agent release all remaining funds to Seller, less pending claims, six months after the Closing Date. Each document reads as normal on its own. Together, any General Representation claim made between month 6 and month 18 has no source of recovery, so the effective survival period is six months. That is too short for problems such as royalty underpayments or post-launch platform compliance failures to surface.
detect_terms: sole and exclusive source of recovery
eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date
issues.expected_finding: Because APA Section 9.6 limits recovery for General Representation breaches to escrow funds then held and Escrow Agreement Section 4.2 releases the escrow six months after Closing, the 18-month survival period in Section 9.1 is effectively cut to six months. The escrow release date should be aligned with the 18-month survival period, or recourse beyond the escrow allowed.
detect_terms2: six (6) months after the Closing Date

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: The APA is governed by Delaware law with exclusive Delaware Chancery jurisdiction (Sections 11.6 and 11.7). APA Section 6.10 requires a Key Employee Agreement with a 24-month non-compete as a Closing deliverable. The Key Employee Agreement is between Treikaith and Fenwright, who lives in Austin, so the APA's precedence clause, which covers only Ancillary Agreements between Buyer and Seller, does not reach it. Section 9.1 of that agreement selects California law and the courts of the County of Los Angeles. Read together with its own Section 6.1 non-compete, that choice of law means California Business and Professions Code Section 16600 (and Section 16600.5) renders the non-compete void. Treikaith therefore loses the restrictive covenant it bargained for to protect the acquired studio's goodwill, and disputes would be split between California and Delaware forums.
detect_terms: laws of the State of California
issues.expected_finding: The Key Employee Agreement's choice of California law and Los Angeles courts conflicts with the APA's Delaware law and Chancery forum, and under California Business and Professions Code Section 16600 it voids the 24-month non-compete that APA Section 6.10 requires. The agreement should be conformed to Delaware (or Texas) law and forum before Closing.

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description: Under APA Section 6.3(b), if Buyer does not deliver a written objection within five Business Days after receiving a Schedule Supplement, the supplement is deemed accepted by Buyer. It is then treated as curing any representation inaccuracy for purposes of Article IX indemnity and the Section 7.2(a) bring-down condition. Supplement No. 1 to the Disclosure Schedule states that it was delivered to Buyer on October 2, 2026, a Friday. It discloses a copyright ownership claim by Orvenna Sound Collective over the Emberfall Saga soundtrack, together with a demand for injunctive relief. Five Business Days from October 2, 2026 ends on October 9, 2026. The recitals of the October 21, 2026 Side Letter record that Buyer objected on October 16, 2026, that Seller contends the supplement was deemed accepted, and that each party reserves its rights. The deadline appears only from reading the APA window against the supplement's delivery date. Treikaith's late objection exposes it to losing both its indemnity and its closing-condition protection for the soundtrack claim, and the Side Letter recital shows the point is still disputed.
issues.expected_finding: Treikaith's October 16, 2026 objection (recorded in the Side Letter recitals) came after the five-Business-Day window under APA Section 6.3(b) closed on October 9, 2026 for the October 2, 2026 Supplement No. 1. Seller can therefore argue the Orvenna soundtrack claim is deemed cured for indemnity and the bring-down condition, so Treikaith should seek an amendment treating its objection as timely or a special indemnity for that claim.

issues.label: defined term inconsistency
issues.description: APA Section 2.1(b) conveys 'Purchased IP', which includes all source code, build tools, unregistered copyrights, art assets and unreleased sequel builds of the Emberfall Saga. The core title representation in APA Section 4.12(a), however, is given only as to 'Assigned IP' and borrows that term's definition from the IP Assignment Agreement. Section 1.1 of the IP Assignment Agreement defines Assigned IP as the registered or applied-for trademarks and copyright registrations set forth on Exhibit A, which is ordinary for a short-form recordation instrument. Each document reads as normal on its own. Together, Seller's title warranty, including its status as a Fundamental Representation, covers only registrations and not the source code and unregistered works that make up most of the value. The APA precedence clause does not cure this because the APA itself adopts the narrower definition.
detect_terms: Seller has good and valid title to all Assigned IP
issues.expected_finding: Because APA Section 4.12(a) warrants title only to 'Assigned IP' as defined in the IP Assignment Agreement, which is limited to registered or applied-for items on Exhibit A, Seller gives no title warranty for the source code, unregistered copyrights and other Purchased IP. Section 4.12(a) should be revised to cover all Purchased IP.

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: Schedule 4.9, Item 3 of the Disclosure Schedule describes the Kestrune Engine License, the engine on which every Emberfall title is built. It requires the prior written consent of Kestrune for any assignment, including by operation of law or in connection with a sale of all or substantially all of the assets of the licensed business. Schedule 2.1(c) lists that license as an Assigned Contract. However, Schedule 4.5 (Required Consents), which APA Section 7.2(d) uses to define the consents that must be obtained before Closing, lists only the console platform publishing agreements and omits Kestrune. Read together, these provisions show that the asset sale triggers Kestrune's consent right, yet no closing condition or covenant addresses it. Treikaith could be obligated to close without a valid engine license, and nothing in the folder records that consent has been obtained.
detect_terms: all or substantially all of the assets
issues.expected_finding: The asset sale triggers Kestrune's consent requirement under the engine license being assigned to Treikaith, but that consent is missing from Schedule 4.5 Required Consents and so from the APA Section 7.2(d) closing condition. Treikaith should add Kestrune's consent as a required consent and closing condition, or obtain a special indemnity, before Closing.
